**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Nobody makes a window out of wool. Nobody makes a sweater out of glass. This week you find out why, and it turns out there is a rule behind it.

1. Read **Why Windows Are Not Wool** with a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Material Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Look at the **Pick the Right Stuff** chart.
4. Play **Which Job Is It For?** and sort the cards.
5. Take **Material Check** — say each answer out loud first.
6. Lock it in with **Remember the Rule**.
7. Read **Material Questions Kids Ask**.
8. Finish with **Investigation: The Spill Test** — find out for yourself which cloth soaks up most.

Your job this week: pick one thing in your home and say why it is made of what it is made of. 🧱

from:
## Why Windows Are Not Wool

Look at a window. Now look at a sweater. Nobody ever mixed those up. Why not?

Every thing is made of some **material**. Glass. Wool. Wood. Metal. Plastic. Each one has its own **properties** — the things you can notice about it.

Glass is **hard**. It is **smooth**. You can see straight through it. Those are exactly what a window needs.

Wool is **soft**. It is **rough** to touch. It traps warm air near your skin. Those are exactly what a sweater needs.

So here is the rule. Somebody picked the material to fit the job.

A raincoat is **waterproof**, so the rain runs off. A towel is the opposite. A towel needs to **absorb** water, which means soak it up. Same water. Two jobs. Two very different materials.

A rubber band is **bendy**, so it stretches and springs back. A brick is not bendy at all, and that is good. You would not want a bendy wall.

How do people know which material to pick? They **test** it. They try each one at the same job and watch what happens. A fair test changes one thing only.

Here is something to notice. One material can be right for one job and wrong for another. Paper is great for drawing. Paper is terrible for a raincoat. The material is not good or bad on its own. It only fits, or does not fit, the job.

Next time you pick something up, ask what it is made of. Then ask why.
to:
## Why Windows Are Not Wool

Look through a clear window. Then feel a soft sweater. Why do people choose different **materials** for these jobs?

A material is what something is made of. Wood, glass, metal, and cloth are materials. 

A **property** is something we can observe or test. Is a sample **hard** or **soft**? Is its surface **rough** or **smooth**? Can we see through it?

Clear glass lets us see outside. It resists dents, but it can still break. Smooth does not always mean see-through: a metal spoon can be smooth too.

A knitted sweater bends with your body. Air held among its fibers helps slow heat escaping from you. Some wool feels soft; some feels scratchy.

A **bendy** strip curves without breaking. A stretchy rubber band gets longer when pulled. Bending and stretching are different.

A raincoat made with **waterproof** material helps keep rain out. A towel needs to **absorb** water, which means take it in. The job helps us choose useful properties.

How do we choose? We **test** real samples. Compare equal-size dry pieces with the same water amount, waiting time, and method. Repeat with fresh dry pieces. Describe what you see.

A damp patch shows where water has spread. A bigger patch does not prove that more water was absorbed. If two samples take in all the water you added, this test cannot tell which could hold more.

Untreated paper towel is useful for spills but poor for a rain cover. A coating can change how paper behaves. Name the exact sample instead of assuming every kind is alike.

Pick an object. What is its job? Which properties help it do that job?

from: Paper towels absorb water instead of keeping it out. An umbrella needs to be waterproof so the rain runs off. The paper would soak through and fall apart, so it is the wrong material for that job.
to: Paper towels take water in and may soak through or tear. A rain cover needs to keep water from passing through. We should test a suitable coated or waterproof sample for that job.

from: Yes. A metal spoon is hard, but a long thin metal wire bends easily. Shape matters too, not just what it is made of. Thin things bend more than thick ones.
to: Yes. A thin metal strip can bend and still be hard to dent. Hardness and flexibility are different properties. Shape and thickness matter too.

from: Mostly from oil, which comes out of the ground. People made the first plastics about a hundred years ago. That is why old toys are wood or metal.
to: Many plastics start with chemicals from oil or gas. Some use plants. Early plastics were made in the 1800s. More kinds came later.

from: It is strong, it is light, it is easy to cut, and trees grow back. For a lot of jobs nothing beats it, which is why houses still use it.
to: Wood can hold things up and be cut to shape. Its kind and thickness matter. Trees take time to grow. We can use wood again and care for forests.

from: Most of it is. Some glass is made cloudy on purpose, for a bathroom window. Same material, changed a little, for a different job.
to: Clear glass lets us see details. Frosted glass lets light through but blurs the view. Smooth does not always mean clear.

from: There is no single winner. Some materials resist squashing best, some resist pulling best, and some bounce back best. Strong at what, is the better question.
to: Ask what the job needs. Pulling, pressing, scratching, and breaking are different tests. Shape and thickness matter too.

from: Often, yes. Glass, metal and paper can be melted or mashed and made into new things. That is what recycling means, and it saves digging up more.
to: Reuse means use an object again. A jar can hold pencils. Recycling turns suitable old material into new products. Glass and metal may be melted. Paper is made into pulp. Check what your local program takes.
